Closest reversible approximation of a Markov chain

Source: R/closestReversible.R
closestReversible.Rd

Finds the Markov chain closest to a given one among the reversible chains, either with respect to a fixed stationary distribution or, with stationaryDistribution = "free", over all stationary distributions.

Usage

closestReversible(
  object,
  stationaryDistribution = NULL,
  tolerance = sqrt(.Machine$double.eps),
  norm = c("pi", "frobenius"),
  nstart = 5L
)

# S4 method for class 'markovchain'
closestReversible(
  object,
  stationaryDistribution = NULL,
  tolerance = sqrt(.Machine$double.eps),
  norm = c("pi", "frobenius"),
  nstart = 5L
)

Arguments

object

A markovchain object representing a finite, irreducible discrete-time Markov chain.

stationaryDistribution

Optional numeric vector giving the stationary distribution \(\pi\) to make the result reversible with respect to, with one strictly positive entry per state (it is normalized if it does not sum to one). With norm = "pi" it must be stationary for object, i.e. satisfy \(\pi P = \pi\), otherwise an error is raised; with norm = "frobenius" any positive distribution is allowed, and the result is the chain nearest to \(P\) among those reversible with respect to it. The default, NULL, uses the chain's own unique stationary distribution from steadyStates. With norm = "frobenius" the string "free" lets the stationary distribution vary as well (see Details).

tolerance

A single finite non-negative number, used when checking that a supplied stationaryDistribution really is stationary (norm = "pi" only). It is a numerical-noise tolerance, not a modelling one.

norm

The distance to minimize: "pi" (the default), the \(\pi\)-weighted Hilbert-Schmidt norm, whose minimizer is the additive reversibilization above; or "frobenius", the plain Frobenius norm \(\|P - R\|_F\), which needs the quadprog package.

nstart

With stationaryDistribution = "free", the number of starting points of the optimization (at least one); ignored otherwise. The first starts from the stationary distribution of object (or the uniform distribution if it is not unique), the second from the uniform distribution, the others from random distributions drawn with the session's random number generator.

Value

A named list with five elements:

chain

The approximating markovchain object \(R\), with the same states and the same row/column-stochastic storage convention as object.

stationaryDistribution

The \(\pi\) with respect to which \(R\) is reversible, as a named numeric vector: the one used or, with "free", the one found.

distance

The distance actually minimized: \(\|P-R\|_\pi\) for norm = "pi", \(\|P-R\|_F\) for norm = "frobenius" (see Details).

frobeniusDistance

The plain Frobenius distance \(\|P-R\|_F\), reported for convenience; with norm = "pi" it is not the quantity being minimized.

norm

The norm used.

With stationaryDistribution = "free" a sixth element, starts, gives for each starting point the Frobenius distance reached.

Details

For a row-stochastic transition matrix \(P\) with stationary distribution \(\pi\), define the time reversal \(P^*\) by $$P^*_{ij} = \frac{\pi_j P_{ji}}{\pi_i}.$$ \(P^*\) is the transition matrix of the same chain run backwards in time, and \(P\) is reversible exactly when \(P = P^*\). With the default norm = "pi" the approximation returned is the additive reversibilization $$R = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(P + P^*\right),$$ which is stochastic, non-negative, and reversible with respect to the same \(\pi\) (see Details). With norm = "frobenius" it is the reversible chain nearest to \(P\) in the plain Frobenius norm, the problem solved by Nielsen and Weber (2015).

In what sense is this the closest chain? With the default norm = "pi", work in the space \(\ell^2(\pi)\) of functions on the states with inner product \(\langle f,g\rangle_\pi=\sum_i \pi_i f_i g_i\). Reversible chains are exactly the self-adjoint operators on that space, and they form a linear subspace. The matching Hilbert-Schmidt inner product on operators is $$\langle A,B\rangle_\pi = \sum_{i,j} \frac{\pi_i}{\pi_j} A_{ij}B_{ij}, \qquad \|A\|_\pi^2 = \sum_{i,j} \frac{\pi_i}{\pi_j} A_{ij}^2,$$ and \(A \mapsto A^*\) is an isometric involution for it. The orthogonal projection onto the fixed points of such an involution is the average of a point and its image, so \(R=(P+P^*)/2\) is the closest \(\pi\)-reversible matrix to \(P\) in \(\|\cdot\|_\pi\). The stochastic and non-negativity constraints come for free: \(P^*\) has row sums \(\sum_j \pi_j P_{ji}/\pi_i = (\pi P)_i/\pi_i = 1\) because \(\pi\) is stationary, and both \(P\) and \(P^*\) are non-negative, so the minimizer over the subspace already lies in the set of transition matrices and no constrained optimization is needed.

The Frobenius norm with a fixed \(\pi\). With norm = "frobenius" the result minimizes \(\|P - R\|_F^2 = \sum_{i,j}(P_{ij} - R_{ij})^2\) over the transition matrices that satisfy detailed balance \(\pi_i R_{ij} = \pi_j R_{ji}\). This is the problem of Nielsen and Weber (2015). Since \(A\mapsto A^*\) is not an isometry of this norm, the additive reversibilization is generally not its solution, and the non-negativity constraints can be active. The problem is a convex quadratic program: with the \(n(n-1)/2\) entries \(R_{ij}\), \(i<j\), as unknowns, \(R_{ji} = \pi_i R_{ij}/\pi_j\) and \(R_{ii} = 1 - \sum_{j\ne i}R_{ij}\), the objective is strictly convex and the constraints are \(R_{ij} \ge 0\) and \(R_{ii} \ge 0\). It is solved exactly by the dual active-set method of quadprog::solve.QP, in \(O(n^6)\) time, which is practical up to about 50 states. \(\pi\) need not be stationary for \(P\); the result is reversible, hence stationary, with respect to it.

Letting \(\pi\) vary. With stationaryDistribution = "free" the minimization is over all reversible chains, whatever their stationary distribution. Every such chain can be written as \(R_{ij} = S_{ij}/\sum_k S_{ik}\) with \(S\) symmetric and non-negative (\(S_{ij} = \pi_i R_{ij}\), the probability flows), so the problem becomes a smooth minimization over \(S \ge 0\), solved with optim(method = "L-BFGS-B") and the analytic gradient. The set of reversible chains is not convex, so the result is a local minimum: nstart starting points are tried, and each local solution is polished by solving the convex problem above at its own \(\pi\), which can only decrease the distance. Nielsen and Weber (2015) keep \(\pi\) fixed; this extension is specific to the package. The distance found is never larger than the one obtained with the stationary distribution of object.

What this function does not do. With norm = "pi" the minimization holds \(\pi\) fixed: the \(\pi\)-weighted norm itself depends on \(\pi\), so letting it vary is only offered for the Frobenius norm. Also, the weighted Frobenius norm of PyDTMC's closest_reversible(weighted = TRUE) is not offered. PyDTMC solves the unweighted problem with an iterative solver, whose solutions agree with the ones here to about \(10^{-5}\) and have a slightly larger distance.

Properties worth knowing. \(R\) has the same stationary distribution \(\pi\) as \(P\), and it preserves the support pattern in the symmetrized sense: \(R_{ij}>0\) whenever \(P_{ij}>0\) or \(P_{ji}>0\). It may therefore allow transitions the original chain forbids, which is inherent to making a chain reversible rather than a defect of this construction. If object is already reversible, \(R=P\) and distance is zero (up to rounding). Fill (1991) introduces this construction, alongside the multiplicative reversibilization \(PP^*\), which is a different object and is not computed here.

Only irreducibility is required, not aperiodicity. Irreducibility guarantees both a unique \(\pi\) and \(\pi_i>0\) for every state, so the division defining \(P^*\) is always safe.

The implementation calls steadyStates at most once and is then \(O(n^2)\) in time and memory for a dense \(n\)-state transition matrix; no eigendecomposition or optimization is involved.

References

Fill, J. A. (1991). Eigenvalue bounds on convergence to stationarity for nonreversible Markov chains, with an application to the exclusion process. The Annals of Applied Probability, 1(1). doi:10.1214/aoap/1177005981

Nielsen, A. and Weber, M. (2015). Computing the nearest reversible Markov chain. Numerical Linear Algebra with Applications, 22. doi:10.1002/nla.1967

See also

is.reversible, steadyStates, is.irreducible

Examples

# A directed 3-cycle is as far from reversible as a chain gets: it only
# ever moves one way round. Its closest reversible approximation is the
# undirected random walk on the same triangle.
statesNames <- c("a", "b", "c")
cycle3 <- new("markovchain", states = statesNames,
  transitionMatrix = matrix(c(0, 1, 0,
                              0, 0, 1,
                              1, 0, 0), byrow = TRUE, nrow = 3,
                            dimnames = list(statesNames, statesNames)))
is.reversible(cycle3)
#> [1] FALSE

approximation <- closestReversible(cycle3)
approximation$chain
#> Unnamed Markov chain (closest reversible) 
#>  A  3 - dimensional discrete Markov Chain defined by the following states: 
#>  a, b, c 
#>  The transition matrix  (by rows)  is defined as follows: 
#>     a   b   c
#> a 0.0 0.5 0.5
#> b 0.5 0.0 0.5
#> c 0.5 0.5 0.0
#> 
is.reversible(approximation$chain)
#> [1] TRUE
approximation$distance
#> [1] 1.224745

# The nearest reversible chain in the Frobenius norm (needs quadprog),
# first with the stationary distribution held fixed, then free.
if (requireNamespace("quadprog", quietly = TRUE)) {
  P <- new("markovchain", states = letters[1:4], transitionMatrix = matrix(
    c(0.1, 0.6, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.15, 0.7, 0.1,
      0.3, 0.05, 0.25, 0.4, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.2), 4, byrow = TRUE,
    dimnames = list(letters[1:4], letters[1:4])))
  closestReversible(P)$frobeniusDistance
  closestReversible(P, norm = "frobenius")$distance
  set.seed(1)
  free <- closestReversible(P, "free", norm = "frobenius")
  free$distance
  free$stationaryDistribution
}
#>          a          b          c          d 
#> 0.20622910 0.29041450 0.40357449 0.09978191
